gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OutdoorGearLab tested both 1 kWh BLUETTIs: the Elite 100 V2 gave 890 Wh (87% of 1,024 Wh) and the AC180 gave 950 Wh. Both now cost $499 at bluettipower.com, so the older AC180 gives 60 Wh more measured energy for the same money but weighs 11 lb more (36 vs 25 lb).
standout_why: I compared against the two cited pages and the PreparedStates roundup, which ranked 14. ChatGPT's answer quotes OutdoorGearLab's AC180 figure (950 Wh) and CNET's Elite 200 V2 figures (81.08% efficiency, 26 h 32 min fridge run, through Yahoo). It gives no measured figure for the Elite 100 V2, the model it recommends. OutdoorGearLab's July 2026 Elite 100 V2 review, with 890 Wh measured, did not appear in ChatGPT's results. PreparedStates says on its own page that it did no hands-on tests: it gives maker figures and a 90%-usable assumption, so about 920 Wh, which is higher than the 890 Wh OutdoorGearLab measured. None of these pages gives a measured idle draw for the Elite 30 V2. The Technology Man measured about 19 W with AC on and Eco off, against BLUETTI's '4.5W standby' claim, and our current page repeats the 4.5 W figure. I could not open the Yahoo/CNET page (HTTP 403). I compared it only as ChatGPT quoted it.
decides: This confirms the Elite 100 V2 as the overall pick only if weight matters. At the same $499, the AC180 measured 950 Wh against 890 Wh in the same reviewer's tests, about 7% more energy. So the current row 'AC180: only at a deep discount' should become 'same price, more measured energy, 11 lb heavier'. For the Elite 30 V2, the CPAP/desk-UPS row should drop '4.5 W standby' or label it as BLUETTI's claim. One named test measured about 19 W with AC on, which would use up its 231 Wh measured AC capacity in about 12 hours with nothing plugged in. The Elite 200 V2 pick holds: two named labs measured 1.91 kWh (StorageReview) and 2,028 Wh (APH Networks) delivered from its 2,073.6 Wh battery.
